claim: T cells engineered to express a tumor-specific αβ T cell receptor (TCR) mediate anti-tumor immunity.
source: T cells engineered to express a tumor-specific αβ T cell receptor (TCR) mediate anti-tumor immunity.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract supported by established scientific knowledge in the field of cancer immunotherapy.

claim: Mispairing of therapeutic αβ chains with endogenous αβ chains reduces therapeutic TCR surface expression.
source: However, mispairing of the therapeutic αβ chains with endogenous αβ chains reduces therapeutic TCR surface expression and generates self-reactive TCRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations in the introduction and by experimental data shown in the manuscript.

claim: Mispairing of therapeutic αβ chains with endogenous αβ chains generates self-reactive TCRs.
source: However, mispairing of the therapeutic αβ chains with endogenous αβ chains reduces therapeutic TCR surface expression and generates self-reactive TCRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations in the introduction and experimental validation in the manuscript.

claim: Domain-swapped TCRs assemble with CD3 when correctly paired.
source: When paired, domain-swapped (ds)TCRs assemble with CD3, express on the cell surface, and mediate antigen-specific T cell responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Domain-swapped TCRs express on the cell surface when correctly paired.
source: When paired, domain-swapped (ds)TCRs assemble with CD3, express on the cell surface, and mediate antigen-specific T cell responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Domain-swapped TCRs mediate antigen-specific T cell responses when correctly paired.
source: When paired, domain-swapped (ds)TCRs assemble with CD3, express on the cell surface, and mediate antigen-specific T cell responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional assay data in Figure 3 and tumor xenograft experiments in Figure 4.

claim: dsTCR chains mispaired with endogenous chains cannot properly assemble with CD3.
source: By contrast, dsTCR chains mispaired with endogenous chains cannot properly assemble with CD3 or signal, preventing autoimmunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 2C-E and 3E showing reduced surface expression of mispaired constructs.

claim: dsTCR chains mispaired with endogenous chains cannot signal.
source: By contrast, dsTCR chains mispaired with endogenous chains cannot properly assemble with CD3 or signal, preventing autoimmunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional assay data in Figure 3G showing lack of IL-2 secretion from mispaired constructs.

claim: Domain-swapped TCRs prevent autoimmunity in a mouse model of TCR gene transfer-induced graft-versus-host disease.
source: We validate this approach in cell-based assays and in a mouse model of TCR gene transfer-induced graft-versus-host disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4C-D showing no TI-GvHD in mice receiving dsTCR-transduced T cells.

claim: The TCR is the sole determinant of T cell specificity.
source: The TCR - a heterodimer that is uniquely rearranged in each T cell during its development - is the sole determinant of T cell specificity (DembiĆ et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to DembiĆ et al., 1986.

claim: Transfer of α and β genes encoding a tumor-reactive αβ TCR can impart anti-tumor reactivity to a cancer patient's T cells.
source: Accordingly, transfer of the α and β genes encoding a tumor-reactive αβ TCR can impart anti-tumor reactivity to a cancer patient's T cells (Clay et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clay et al., 1999.

claim: TCR-engineered T cells mediate potent anti-tumor cytotoxicity upon reinfusion into the patient.
source: Upon reinfusion into the patient, these engineered T cells mediate potent anti-tumor cytotoxicity (Park et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Park et al., 2011.

claim: TCR gene therapy has demonstrated clinical responses for several malignancies.
source: This approach – termed TCR gene therapy – has demonstrated clinical responses for several malignancies (Johnson et al., 2009; Morgan et al., 2006; Davis, 2010; Parkhurst, 2011; Robbins et al., 2015, 2011), which may be bolstered in the future through combination with complementary immunotherapies like dendritic cell-based vaccination and checkpoint blockade (Abate-Daga et al., 2013; Brahmer and Hammers, 2015; Mellman et al., 2011; Sharma and Allison, 2015; Topalian et al., 2015; Chodon, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: TCR chain mispairing reduces the level of correctly-paired, tumor-reactive TCR heterodimers expressed on the T cell surface.
source: TCR chain mispairing reduces the level of correctly-paired, tumor-reactive TCR heterodimers expressed on the T cell surface, possibly reducing therapeutic efficacy (Jorritsma et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jorritsma et al., 2007.

claim: Mispairing can generate self-reactive TCR heterodimers that do not undergo thymic negative selection.
source: More ominously, mispairing can generate self-reactive TCR heterodimers that do not undergo thymic negative selection.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the mechanism of TCR mispairing and thymic selection processes.

claim: Mispaired TCRs engender autoreactivity in TCR-transduced human T cells in vitro.
source: These mispaired TCRs engender autoreactivity in TCR-transduced human T cells in vitro (van Loenen et al., 2010) and mediate lethal graft-versus-host disease in mice administered TCR-transduced T cells following a protocol mimicking human clinical trials (Bendle et al., 2010; Bunse, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to van Loenen et al., 2010.

claim: Mispaired TCRs mediate lethal graft-versus-host disease in mice administered TCR-transduced T cells following a protocol mimicking human clinical trials.
source: These mispaired TCRs engender autoreactivity in TCR-transduced human T cells in vitro (van Loenen et al., 2010) and mediate lethal graft-versus-host disease in mice administered TCR-transduced T cells following a protocol mimicking human clinical trials (Bendle et al., 2010; Bunse, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bendle et al., 2010 and Bunse, 2014.

claim: No serious adverse events have been attributed to TCR mispairing in engineered T cell trials.
source: Although no serious adverse events have been attributed to TCR mispairing in engineered T cell trials (Rosenberg, 2010), autoreactive off-target and off-tumor engineered T cell responses have caused deaths (Linette et al., 2013; Morgan et al., 2013, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rosenberg, 2010.

claim: Autoreactive off-target and off-tumor engineered T cell responses have caused deaths.
source: Although no serious adverse events have been attributed to TCR mispairing in engineered T cell trials (Rosenberg, 2010), autoreactive off-target and off-tumor engineered T cell responses have caused deaths (Linette et al., 2013; Morgan et al., 2013, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Linette et al., 2013 and Morgan et al., 2013, 2010.

claim: The TCR α and β chains each contain a membrane-distal variable immunoglobulin domain (V), which imparts specificity.
source: The TCR α and β chains each contain a membrane-distal variable immunoglobulin domain (V), which imparts specificity, and several constant domains including a membrane-proximal constant immunoglobulin domain (C), a connecting peptide (cp), a transmembrane helix (TM), and a short cytoplasmic tail (cyto) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TCR structure, also illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The TCR αβ heterodimer must assemble with six additional chains (CD3 dimers γε, δε, and ζ2) to achieve functional form.
source: To achieve functional form, the TCR αβ heterodimer must assemble with six additional chains (CD3 dimers γε, δε, and ζ2), which facilitate export of the TCR complex to the cell surface and mediate signal transduction upon antigen binding (Call and Wucherpfennig, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Call and Wucherpfennig, 2005.

claim: CD3 chains facilitate export of the TCR complex to the cell surface.
source: To achieve functional form, the TCR αβ heterodimer must assemble with six additional chains (CD3 dimers γε, δε, and ζ2), which facilitate export of the TCR complex to the cell surface and mediate signal transduction upon antigen binding (Call and Wucherpfennig, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Call and Wucherpfennig, 2005.

claim: CD3 chains mediate signal transduction upon antigen binding.
source: To achieve functional form, the TCR αβ heterodimer must assemble with six additional chains (CD3 dimers γε, δε, and ζ2), which facilitate export of the TCR complex to the cell surface and mediate signal transduction upon antigen binding (Call and Wucherpfennig, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Call and Wucherpfennig, 2005.

claim: If the TCR/CD3 complex is not assembled properly prior to export, it is degraded.
source: If the TCR/CD3 complex is not assembled properly prior to export, it is degraded (Bonifacino, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bonifacino, 1989.

claim: Assembly with CD3 requires contacts within the constant domains of both the TCR α and β chains.
source: Assembly with CD3 requires contacts within the constant domains of both the TCR α and β chains (Call et al., 2002; Kuhns and Davis, 2007; Xu and Call, 2006), most critically the basic residues within the transmembrane domains (Call et al., 2002)(Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Call et al., 2002; Kuhns and Davis, 2007; Xu and Call, 2006, and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Basic residues within the transmembrane domains are most critical for assembly with CD3.
source: Assembly with CD3 requires contacts within the constant domains of both the TCR α and β chains (Call et al., 2002; Kuhns and Davis, 2007; Xu and Call, 2006), most critically the basic residues within the transmembrane domains (Call et al., 2002)(Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Call et al., 2002 and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The dsTCRV construct did not bind tetramer.
source: The dsTCRV construct did not bind tetramer (Figure 2B), and variation of the precise position at which the V domains were exchanged did not rectify this (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Both F5 dsTCRC and dsTCRcp bound tetramer.
source: However, both F5 dsTCRC and dsTCRcp bound tetramer, indicating these architectures express on the cell surface and retain specificity for their cognate ligand (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cells transfected with F5 dsTCRC bound tetramer with comparable avidity to wtTCR.
source: Cells transfected with F5 dsTCRC bound tetramer with comparable avidity to wtTCR, whereas tetramer binding for dsTCRcp was lower.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Tetramer binding for F5 dsTCRcp was lower than wtTCR.
source: Cells transfected with F5 dsTCRC bound tetramer with comparable avidity to wtTCR, whereas tetramer binding for dsTCRcp was lower.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Surface expression of simulated mispaired constructs was significantly reduced compared to fully wtTCR or dsTCRC.
source: As expected, compared to fully wtTCR or dsTCRC, surface expression of these simulated mispaired constructs was significantly reduced, indicating impaired assembly of CD3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: dsTCR derivatives of M1 and 1G4 human TCRs express on the surface of CD3+ 293T.
source: For both additional human TCRs as well as the murine TCR, dsTCR derivatives express on the surface of CD3+ 293T and mitigate mispairing with wtTCR chains (Figure 2D,E), suggesting this approach can be applied generally to human and mouse TCRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: dsTCR derivatives of OTI murine TCR express on the surface of CD3+ 293T.
source: For both additional human TCRs as well as the murine TCR, dsTCR derivatives express on the surface of CD3+ 293T and mitigate mispairing with wtTCR chains (Figure 2D,E), suggesting this approach can be applied generally to human and mouse TCRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: dsTCR derivatives mitigate mispairing with wtTCR chains.
source: For both additional human TCRs as well as the murine TCR, dsTCR derivatives express on the surface of CD3+ 293T and mitigate mispairing with wtTCR chains (Figure 2D,E), suggesting this approach can be applied generally to human and mouse TCRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: The domain-swapping approach can be applied generally to human and mouse TCRs.
source: For both additional human TCRs as well as the murine TCR, dsTCR derivatives express on the surface of CD3+ 293T and mitigate mispairing with wtTCR chains (Figure 2D,E), suggesting this approach can be applied generally to human and mouse TCRs.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 2D,E testing multiple TCRs.

claim: CD3ε-EpoR drove proliferation of BaF3 cells when complexed with wtTCR, dsTCRC, or dsTCRcp.
source: Following removal of IL-3 from the cell media, εE drove proliferation of BaF3 cells when complexed with wtTCR, dsTCRC, or dsTCRcp, indicating that dsTCRs assemble with CD3 chains in the same orientation as wtTCR (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: dsTCRs assemble with CD3 chains in the same orientation as wtTCR.
source: Following removal of IL-3 from the cell media, εE drove proliferation of BaF3 cells when complexed with wtTCR, dsTCRC, or dsTCRcp, indicating that dsTCRs assemble with CD3 chains in the same orientation as wtTCR (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the BaF3 proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both dsTCRC and dsTCRcp assemble endogenous CD3 in Jurkat T cells.
source: Both dsTCRC and dsTCRcp assemble endogenous CD3, express on the cell surface, and bind cognate A2/MART1 multimers to an extent similar to the wtTCR (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: dsTCRC and dsTCRcp express on the cell surface of Jurkat T cells.
source: Both dsTCRC and dsTCRcp assemble endogenous CD3, express on the cell surface, and bind cognate A2/MART1 multimers to an extent similar to the wtTCR (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: dsTCRC and dsTCRcp bind cognate A2/MART1 multimers to an extent similar to the wtTCR in Jurkat T cells.
source: Both dsTCRC and dsTCRcp assemble endogenous CD3, express on the cell surface, and bind cognate A2/MART1 multimers to an extent similar to the wtTCR (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Hybrid constructs comprising one dsTCR chain and one wtTCR chain were not detectable on the surface of transduced Jurkat cells.
source: By contrast, hybrid constructs comprising one dsTCR chain and one wtTCR chain were not detectable on the surface of transduced Jurkat cells, indicating that, as expected, these mispaired constructs failed to form a mature complex (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Mispaired constructs failed to form a mature complex in Jurkat cells.
source: By contrast, hybrid constructs comprising one dsTCR chain and one wtTCR chain were not detectable on the surface of transduced Jurkat cells, indicating that, as expected, these mispaired constructs failed to form a mature complex (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of surface expression shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Virtually all transduced (Myc271+) Jurkat cells were positive for A2/MART1 staining.
source: Virtually all transduced (Myc271+) cells were positive for A2/MART1 staining (Figure 3F), indicating the dsTCRs competed favorably for CD3 recruitment in the presence of the endogenous Jurkat TCR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: dsTCRs competed favorably for CD3 recruitment in the presence of the endogenous Jurkat TCR.
source: Virtually all transduced (Myc271+) cells were positive for A2/MART1 staining (Figure 3F), indicating the dsTCRs competed favorably for CD3 recruitment in the presence of the endogenous Jurkat TCR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high percentage of transduced cells expressing functional TCR shown in Figure 3F.

claim: dsTCRs mediated antigen-specific release of IL-2 from Jurkat T cells.
source: Consistent with multimer staining results, dsTCRs mediated antigen-specific release of IL-2, whereas hybrid wt/dsTCRs simulating mispairing did not (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Hybrid wt/dsTCRs simulating mispairing did not mediate antigen-specific release of IL-2 from Jurkat T cells.
source: Consistent with multimer staining results, dsTCRs mediated antigen-specific release of IL-2, whereas hybrid wt/dsTCRs simulating mispairing did not (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: wtTCR was detected in only 74% of transduced (LNGFR+) primary T cells.
source: As expected, wtTCR was detected in only a subset (74%) of transduced (LNGFR+) cells, indicating ~25% of T cells express an endogenous TCR that out-competes F5 TCR for CD3 recruitment and cell surface expression (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Approximately 25% of primary T cells express an endogenous TCR that out-competes F5 TCR for CD3 recruitment and cell surface expression.
source: As expected, wtTCR was detected in only a subset (74%) of transduced (LNGFR+) cells, indicating ~25% of T cells express an endogenous TCR that out-competes F5 TCR for CD3 recruitment and cell surface expression (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is an inference based on the percentage of transduced cells expressing wtTCR shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Dextramer staining was lower for dsTCRs than wtTCRs in primary T cells.
source: Dextramer staining was lower for dsTCRs than wtTCRs in primary T cells (25% and 11% of LNGFR+ cells, for dsTCRC and dsTCRcp, respectively; MFI = 21% and 13% that of wtTCR).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: A larger subset of endogenous TCRs outcompete the dsTCRs for CD3 recruitment compared to wtTCR.
source: This indicates a larger subset of endogenous TCRs outcompete the dsTCRs for CD3 recruitment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lower dextramer staining for dsTCRs compared to wtTCR in primary T cells.

claim: T cells transduced with either wtTCR or dsTCRs were functional, secreting IFN-γ in an antigen-specific manner.
source: Nonetheless, T cells transduced with either wtTCR or dsTCRs were functional, secreting IFN-γ and upregulating cell surface CD25 in an antigen-specific manner when coincubated with target cells (Figure 3I,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I,J.

claim: T cells transduced with either wtTCR or dsTCRs upregulated cell surface CD25 in an antigen-specific manner.
source: Nonetheless, T cells transduced with either wtTCR or dsTCRs were functional, secreting IFN-γ and upregulating cell surface CD25 in an antigen-specific manner when coincubated with target cells (Figure 3I,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I,J.

claim: Simulated mispaired constructs did not elicit T cell activation in primary T cells.
source: As with Jurkat cells, simulated mispaired constructs elicited no such activation (Figure 3I,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I,J.

claim: dsTCRs assemble with endogenous CD3 to mediate antigen-specific immunity in primary lymphocytes.
source: Thus, dsTCRs assemble with endogenous CD3 to mediate antigen-specific immunity in primary lymphocytes and are rendered nonfunctional when mispaired with wtTCR chains.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: dsTCRs are rendered nonfunctional when mispaired with wtTCR chains.
source: Thus, dsTCRs assemble with endogenous CD3 to mediate antigen-specific immunity in primary lymphocytes and are rendered nonfunctional when mispaired with wtTCR chains.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The wtα and wtβ chains of F5 TCR mispaired with endogenous TCR chains in 88% and 58% of transduced T cells, respectively.
source: The wtα and wtβ chains of F5 TCR mispaired with endogenous TCR chains in 88% and 58% of transduced T cells, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Neither dsα nor dsβ chains of F5 TCR exhibited detectable mispairing with endogenous TCR chains.
source: By contrast, neither dsα nor dsβ chains exhibited detectable mispairing with endogenous TCR chains (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: wtα and wtβ chains of OTI TCR were mispaired in 63% and 84% of transduced murine T cells.
source: Similar results were obtained with the murine OTI TCR: wtα and wtβ chains were mispaired in 63% and 84% of transduced murine T cells, whereas mispairing was not observed with dsα or dsβ chains (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mispairing was not observed with dsα or dsβ chains of OTI TCR.
source: Similar results were obtained with the murine OTI TCR: wtα and wtβ chains were mispaired in 63% and 84% of transduced murine T cells, whereas mispairing was not observed with dsα or dsβ chains (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: dsTCR chains exhibit no detectable mispairing with endogenous TCR chains even when transduced individually.
source: Thus, even when mispairing propensity is maximized by transduction of a single dsTCR chain in the absence of stoichiometric expression of its correct partner, dsTCR chains exhibit no detectable mispairing with endogenous TCR chains.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Mice that received wtTCR(IRES)-transduced T cells exhibited significant cachexia following IL-2 administration.
source: Indeed, mice that received wtTCR(IRES)-transduced T cells - in which the transduced wtTCR chains were linked by an internal ribosome entry site (IRES) sequence – exhibited significant cachexia following IL-2 administration (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 47% (7/15) of mice that received wtTCR(IRES)-transduced T cells developed TI-GvHD to an extent that necessitated euthanasia.
source: Although some of these mice regained weight and survived, 47% (7/15) developed TI-GvHD to an extent that necessitated euthanasia (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Replacing the IRES with a viral 2A sequence reduced but did not eliminate the incidence of TI-GvHD.
source: Consistent with previous results (Bendle et al., 2010), the incidence of TI-GvHD could be reduced but not eliminated by replacing the IRES with a viral 2A sequence to ensure stoichiometric expression of the wtTCR chains.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and a citation to Bendle et al., 2010.

claim: Only 1/15 mice in the wtTCR(2A) group developed fatal TI-GvHD.
source: In this wtTCR(2A) group, less weight loss was observed and only 1/15 mice developed fatal TI-GvHD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cachexia was not observed for mice that received dsTCRC(2A)-transduced T cells.
source: By contrast, cachexia was not observed for mice that received dsTCRC(2A)-transduced T cells, and none (0/25) of these mice developed TI-GvHD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: None (0/25) of mice that received dsTCRC(2A)-transduced T cells developed TI-GvHD.
source: By contrast, cachexia was not observed for mice that received dsTCRC(2A)-transduced T cells, and none (0/25) of these mice developed TI-GvHD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: dsTCRs prevent mispairing and thereby prevent mispairing-related autoimmune complications in a model of TCR gene therapy.
source: Thus, dsTCRs prevent mispairing and thereby prevent mispairing-related autoimmune complications in a model of TCR gene therapy.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mouse T cells transduced with OTI wtTCR or dsTCRC produced a similar complement of cytokines upon stimulation with cognate peptide-MHC multimer.
source: Mouse T cells transduced with OTI wtTCR or dsTCRC produced a similar complement of cytokines upon stimulation with cognate peptide-MHC multimer (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Vα2+/Vβ5+ T cells were present in the spleen for at least 6 weeks following T cell injection.
source: For at least 6 weeks following T cell injection, Vα2+/Vβ5+ T cells were present in the spleen and retained specificity for H-2Kb/Ova tetramer (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Vα2+/Vβ5+ T cells retained specificity for H-2Kb/Ova tetramer for at least 6 weeks following T cell injection.
source: For at least 6 weeks following T cell injection, Vα2+/Vβ5+ T cells were present in the spleen and retained specificity for H-2Kb/Ova tetramer (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Splenic T cells exhibited antigen-specific IFN-γ release upon stimulation with ovalbumin peptide ex vivo.
source: These splenic T cells exhibited antigen-specific IFN-γ release and modulated the surface expression of T cell activation markers upon stimulation with ovalbumin peptide ex vivo (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Splenic T cells modulated the surface expression of T cell activation markers upon stimulation with ovalbumin peptide ex vivo.
source: These splenic T cells exhibited antigen-specific IFN-γ release and modulated the surface expression of T cell activation markers upon stimulation with ovalbumin peptide ex vivo (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: E.G7 tumor grew in all control mice injected with LNGFR-transduced T cells.
source: The ovalbumin-expressing murine thymoma line, E.G7, grew in all control mice injected with LNGFR-transduced T cells, but did not grow detectably in any mice injected with either wtTCR- or dsTCR-transduced T cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: E.G7 tumor did not grow detectably in any mice injected with either wtTCR- or dsTCR-transduced T cells.
source: The ovalbumin-expressing murine thymoma line, E.G7, grew in all control mice injected with LNGFR-transduced T cells, but did not grow detectably in any mice injected with either wtTCR- or dsTCR-transduced T cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Tumor cell killing by dsTCR-transduced T cells was antigen-specific.
source: Tumor cell killing was antigen-specific, because EL4 – the ovalbumin-negative parental line from which E.G7 was derived – grew readily in mice injected with dsTCR-transduced T cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Both wtTCR- and dsTCR-transduced T cells slowed tumor growth when mice were injected with 1 T cell per 500 tumor cells.
source: Both wtTCR- and dsTCR-transduced T cells slowed tumor growth when mice were injected with 1 T cell per 500 tumor cells, and prevented tumor growth entirely at higher tested ratios (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Both wtTCR- and dsTCR-transduced T cells prevented tumor growth entirely at higher T cell to tumor cell ratios.
source: Both wtTCR- and dsTCR-transduced T cells slowed tumor growth when mice were injected with 1 T cell per 500 tumor cells, and prevented tumor growth entirely at higher tested ratios (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: dsTCRs mediate antigen-specific immunity but not deleterious autoimmunity in vivo.
source: Thus, dsTCRs mediate antigen-specific immunity but not deleterious autoimmunity in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: RNAi-mediated silencing of endogenous TCR genes improves surface expression of a co-delivered codon-optimized TCR.
source: A recent report demonstrated that RNAi-mediated silencing of endogenous TCR genes improves surface expression and reduces mispairing of a co-delivered codon-optimized TCR (Bunse, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bunse, 2014.

claim: RNAi-mediated silencing of endogenous TCR genes reduces mispairing of a co-delivered codon-optimized TCR.
source: A recent report demonstrated that RNAi-mediated silencing of endogenous TCR genes improves surface expression and reduces mispairing of a co-delivered codon-optimized TCR (Bunse, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bunse, 2014.

claim: TI-GvHD was not eliminated entirely by RNAi-mediated silencing of endogenous TCR, indicating incomplete knockdown of endogenous TCR.
source: However, TI-GvHD was not eliminated entirely, indicating incomplete knockdown of endogenous TCR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the persistence of TI-GvHD despite shRNA knockdown.

claim: The β chain (Vβ8) of P14 wtTCR was disproportionally detected on the cell surface relative to the α chain (Vα2).
source: As previously shown (Bunse, 2014), the β chain (Vβ8) of P14 wtTCR was disproportionally detected on the cell surface relative to the α chain (Vα2) - indicative of mispairing - even when translational stoichiometry was ensured through the use of a viral 2A sequence (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and a citation to Bunse, 2014.

claim: Co-delivery of shRNA resulted in knockdown of endogenous TCR surface expression to ~40% of normal levels.
source: Co-delivery of shRNA resulted in knockdown of endogenous TCR surface expression to ~40% of normal levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), improving the balance of P14 wtTCR chains expressed on the surface and increasing tetramer staining (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Co-delivery of shRNA improved the balance of P14 wtTCR chains expressed on the surface.
source: Co-delivery of shRNA resulted in knockdown of endogenous TCR surface expression to ~40% of normal levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), improving the balance of P14 wtTCR chains expressed on the surface and increasing tetramer staining (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Co-delivery of shRNA increased tetramer staining of P14 wtTCR.
source: Co-delivery of shRNA resulted in knockdown of endogenous TCR surface expression to ~40% of normal levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), improving the balance of P14 wtTCR chains expressed on the surface and increasing tetramer staining (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The domain-swapped α and β chains of P14 TCR were detected in equal amounts on the cell surface with or without endogenous TCR knockdown.
source: Reflecting the lack of mispairing exhibited by dsTCRs, the domain-swapped α and β chains were detected in equal amounts on the cell surface with or without endogenous TCR knockdown (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Endogenous TCR knockdown greatly improved surface expression of the P14 dsTCR by reducing competition for assembly with CD3 chains.
source: However, knockdown greatly improved surface expression and tetramer binding of the P14 dsTCR by reducing competition for assembly with CD3 chains (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Endogenous TCR knockdown greatly improved tetramer binding of the P14 dsTCR.
source: However, knockdown greatly improved surface expression and tetramer binding of the P14 dsTCR by reducing competition for assembly with CD3 chains (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Mice injected with P14 wtTCR-transduced T cells exhibited weight loss and developed TI-GvHD.
source: Mice injected with P14 wtTCR-transduced T cells exhibited weight loss and developed TI-GvHD, which was prevented by co-delivery of shRNA (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: TI-GvHD from P14 wtTCR-transduced T cells was prevented by co-delivery of shRNA.
source: Mice injected with P14 wtTCR-transduced T cells exhibited weight loss and developed TI-GvHD, which was prevented by co-delivery of shRNA (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: No TI-GvHD was observed in mice receiving P14 dsTCR-transduced T cells, whether or not shRNAs were co-delivered.
source: By contrast, no TI-GvHD was observed in mice receiving P14 dsTCR-transduced T cells, whether or not shRNAs were co-delivered.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: P14 dsTCR did not induce TI-GvHD because the P14 domain-swapped α and β chains did not mispair with endogenous chains.
source: As with OTI dsTCR (Figure 4B), P14 dsTCR did not induce TI-GvHD because the P14 domain-swapped α and β chains did not mispair with endogenous chains (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: Individually delivered P14 wild-type α and β chains mispaired with endogenous chains even when both endogenous chains were knocked down.
source: By contrast, individually delivered P14 wild-type α and β chains mispaired with endogenous chains even when both endogenous chains were knocked down.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: Knockdown of both endogenous chains increased mispairing of P14 wtα.
source: In fact, knockdown of both endogenous chains increased mispairing of P14 wtα, suggesting the reduction of competing endogenous α enabled more mispairing of the weak P14 wtα with the remaining endogenous β chain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F and inference about the mechanism.

claim: A combination approach of endogenous TCR knockdown and dsTCR transduction may optimize safety and efficacy over either approach alone.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that a combination approach of endogenous TCR knockdown and dsTCR transduction may optimize safety and efficacy over either approach alone.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the experimental results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Hematopoietic stem cells transduced with pre-rearranged TCR genes differentiate into antigen-specific T cells in the periphery.
source: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) transduced with pre-rearranged TCR genes differentiate into antigen-specific T cells in the periphery (Vatakis et al., 2011; Yang and Baltimore, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vatakis et al., 2011 and Yang and Baltimore, 2005.

claim: Expression of a pre-rearranged TCR in HSCs suppresses rearrangement of the endogenous TCR in these cells via allelic exclusion.
source: Additionally, expression of a pre-rearranged TCR in HSCs suppresses rearrangement of the endogenous TCR in these cells via allelic exclusion (Hinrichs et al., 2013; Vatakis, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hinrichs et al., 2013 and Vatakis, 2013.

claim: Allelic exclusion in TCR-transduced HSCs is incomplete.
source: As allelic exclusion in TCR-transduced HSCs is incomplete, however, there remains a risk that TCR mispairing can precipitate autoimmunity.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation in the field.

claim: A2/MART1-specific CD3ε+ T cells constituted up to 87.7% of human CD45+ thymocytes in mice engrafted with dsTCR-transduced stem cells.
source: Three months after injection, A2/MART1-specific CD3ε+ T cells constituted up to 87.7% of human CD45+ thymocytes and up to 66.7% of human CD45+ CD19- CD3ε+ splenocytes in mice engrafted with dsTCR-transduced stem cells (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: A2/MART1-specific CD3ε+ T cells constituted up to 66.7% of human CD45+ CD19- CD3ε+ splenocytes in mice engrafted with dsTCR-transduced stem cells.
source: Three months after injection, A2/MART1-specific CD3ε+ T cells constituted up to 87.7% of human CD45+ thymocytes and up to 66.7% of human CD45+ CD19- CD3ε+ splenocytes in mice engrafted with dsTCR-transduced stem cells (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: dsTCRs are compatible with TCR-engineered HSC adoptive transfer.
source: Therefore, dsTCRs are compatible with TCR-engineered HSC adoptive transfer.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: αβ TCR chains transduced into γδ T cells do not mispair with endogenous γδ TCR chains.
source: Interestingly, αβ TCR chains transduced into γδ T cells do not mispair with endogenous γδ TCR chains (Saito, 1988; van der Veken et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Saito, 1988 and van der Veken et al., 2006.

claim: αβ TCR-transduced γδ T cells mediate antigen-specific immunity in vitro and in mouse models.
source: These αβ TCR-transduced γδ T cells mediate antigen-specific immunity in vitro and in mouse models (van der Veken et al., 2006, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to van der Veken et al., 2006, 2009.

claim: Chimeric domain-swapping at the V-C junction resulted in loss of TCR surface expression.
source: As with the interchain domain-swapped constructs (Figure 2B), chimeric domain-swapping at the V-C junction resulted in loss of TCR surface expression (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Both dsTCRδγ and dsTCRγδ expressed on the surface and bound cognate dextramer to a similar extent as wtTCR in Jurkat T cells.
source: By contrast, both dsTCRδγ and dsTCRγδ expressed on the surface and bound cognate dextramer to a similar extent as wtTCR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Three of the four simulated mispaired constructs comprising one chimeric chain and one wtTCR chain did not bind dextramer.
source: As expected, 3 of the 4 simulated mispaired constructs comprising one chimeric chain and one wtTCR chain did not bind dextramer (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: The wtα/dsβγ mispaired construct was detected at a low level on the cell surface, binding dextramer at 20% the level of wtTCR.
source: Only the wtα/dsβγ mispaired construct was detected at a low level on the cell surface, binding dextramer at 20% the level of wtTCR (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Chimeric dsTCRδγ and dsTCRγδ assemble with CD3 chains with similar efficiency as wtTCR in the presence of competing endogenous TCR in primary T cells.
source: Dextramer binding results were similar in primary T cells, indicating that chimeric dsTCRδγ and dsTCRγδ assemble with CD3 chains with similar efficiency as wtTCR in the presence of competing endogenous TCR (Figure 7F; MFI for dsTCRδγ and dsTCRγδ = 157% and 174% that of wtTCR, respectively).
evidence: This is an inference based on dextramer binding data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: T cells expressing chimeric dsTCRs were activated and secreted IFN-γ in response to coincubation with cognate antigen-expressing target cells.
source: T cells expressing chimeric dsTCRs were activated and secreted IFN-γ in response to coincubation with cognate antigen-expressing target cells (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G,H.

claim: Functional outputs of chimeric dsTCRs were reduced relative to wtTCR, indicating chimeric domain-swapping partially impaired signaling capacity.
source: In contrast to dextramer binding, these functional outputs were reduced for chimeric dsTCRs relative to wtTCR, indicating chimeric domain-swapping partially impaired signaling capacity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional assay data shown in Figure 7G,H.

claim: Chimeric dsαδ, dsαγ, and dsβδ chains did not mispair productively with wild-type αβ TCR chains in primary T cells.
source: As observed in Jurkats, chimeric dsαδ, dsαγ, and dsβδ chains did not mispair productively with wild-type αβ TCR chains (Figure 7F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F-H.

claim: The wtα/dsβγ mispaired construct exhibited low levels of dextramer binding (7% of wt) and secreted IFN-γ (20% of wt).
source: Only the wtα/dsβγ mispaired construct exhibited low levels of dextramer binding (7% of wt) and secreted IFN-γ (20% of wt), indicating some allowance for pairing between constant TCRα and TCRγ domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F-H.

claim: There is some allowance for pairing between constant TCRα and TCRγ domains.
source: Only the wtα/dsβγ mispaired construct exhibited low levels of dextramer binding (7% of wt) and secreted IFN-γ (20% of wt), indicating some allowance for pairing between constant TCRα and TCRγ domains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the residual function of the wtα/dsβγ mispaired construct.

claim: Substitution of constant domains of tumor-specific αβ TCRs with corresponding γδ TCR domains produces a chimeric receptor that mediates functional, antigen-specific T cell immunity with minimized mispairing risk.
source: Thus, substitution of constant domains of tumor-specific αβ TCRs with corresponding γδ TCR domains produces a chimeric receptor that mediates functional, antigen-specific T cell immunity with minimized mispairing risk.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Mispairing between introduced and endogenous TCR chains produces autoreactive human T cells in vitro.
source: However, mispairing between introduced and endogenous TCR chains produces autoreactive human T cells in vitro (van Loenen et al., 2010) and causes graft-vs-host disease in mice (Bendle et al., 2010; Bunse, 2014), indicating that TCR gene transfer poses a non-theoretical risk of autoimmunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to van Loenen et al., 2010.

claim: Mispairing between introduced and endogenous TCR chains causes graft-vs-host disease in mice.
source: However, mispairing between introduced and endogenous TCR chains produces autoreactive human T cells in vitro (van Loenen et al., 2010) and causes graft-vs-host disease in mice (Bendle et al., 2010; Bunse, 2014), indicating that TCR gene transfer poses a non-theoretical risk of autoimmunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bendle et al., 2010 and Bunse, 2014.

claim: TCR gene transfer poses a non-theoretical risk of autoimmunity.
source: However, mispairing between introduced and endogenous TCR chains produces autoreactive human T cells in vitro (van Loenen et al., 2010) and causes graft-vs-host disease in mice (Bendle et al., 2010; Bunse, 2014), indicating that TCR gene transfer poses a non-theoretical risk of autoimmunity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited evidence of autoreactivity in vitro and in vivo.

claim: dsTCR chains mispair with wtTCR chains inefficiently due to juxtaposition of non-interacting domains.
source: Interchain domain-swapped TCRs prevent mispairing-related autoreactivity through three potential mechanisms: (1) dsTCR chains mispair with wtTCR chains inefficiently due to juxtaposition of non-interacting domains (i.e. neither α nor β self-associate); (2) mispairing between wt and ds chains results in a receptor that incompletely assembles with CD3 chains and is degraded; (3) mispaired wt/dsTCRs that escape degradation and express on the surface with an incomplete complement of CD3 chains will have impaired signaling capacity.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the structural design of dsTCRs.

claim: Mispairing between wt and ds chains results in a receptor that incompletely assembles with CD3 chains and is degraded.
source: Interchain domain-swapped TCRs prevent mispairing-related autoreactivity through three potential mechanisms: (1) dsTCR chains mispair with wtTCR chains inefficiently due to juxtaposition of non-interacting domains (i.e. neither α nor β self-associate); (2) mispairing between wt and ds chains results in a receptor that incompletely assembles with CD3 chains and is degraded; (3) mispaired wt/dsTCRs that escape degradation and express on the surface with an incomplete complement of CD3 chains will have impaired signaling capacity.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by experimental data showing reduced surface expression of mispaired constructs.

claim: Mispaired wt/dsTCRs that escape degradation and express on the surface with an incomplete complement of CD3 chains will have impaired signaling capacity.
source: Interchain domain-swapped TCRs prevent mispairing-related autoreactivity through three potential mechanisms: (1) dsTCR chains mispair with wtTCR chains inefficiently due to juxtaposition of non-interacting domains (i.e. neither α nor β self-associate); (2) mispairing between wt and ds chains results in a receptor that incompletely assembles with CD3 chains and is degraded; (3) mispaired wt/dsTCRs that escape degradation and express on the surface with an incomplete complement of CD3 chains will have impaired signaling capacity.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by experimental data showing lack of function of mispaired constructs.

claim: Proper dsTCR/CD3 complex assembly is central to the differential function of correctly paired versus mispaired dsTCRs.
source: Thus, proper dsTCR/CD3 complex assembly is central to the differential function of correctly paired versus mispaired dsTCRs.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the proposed mechanisms and experimental data.

claim: dsTCRs assemble with CD3 chains with proper juxtaposition of CD3ε chains.
source: Despite this, dsTCRs assemble with CD3 chains with proper juxtaposition of CD3ε chains, express on the cell surface, and mediate functional, antigen-specific responses, including tumor cell killing.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: dsTCR/CD3 complexes preserve the transmembrane contacts between the TCR and CD3 chains that are essential for complex assembly.
source: This indicates that dsTCR/CD3 complexes preserve the transmembrane contacts between the TCR and CD3 chains that are essential for complex assembly (Call et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional assembly of dsTCRs with CD3 and a citation to Call et al., 2002.

claim: The domain-swapping approach can be applied broadly to TCRs of therapeutic interest.
source: Finally, although we focus on TCRs relevant to cancer immunotherapy, domain-swapping was applied successfully to all TCRs attempted, including four human TCRs and two mouse TCRs. Thus, the general dsTCR approach can be applied broadly to TCRs of therapeutic interest, enabling development of safer immunotherapies for a variety of cancers, infections, and autoimmune diseases.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data testing multiple TCRs.
